details: IAEA Safety Standards GS-R-2 (2002): Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ) inner zone (precautionary action zone, PAZ): typically 3-5 km radius; area where immediate protective actions (sheltering, KI, evacuation) can be taken before release; Soviet standard 1986: 3km immediate zone + 30km monitoring zone; Chernobyl: 3km zone established April 26 evening; inadequate (contamination extended 10+ km in NW sector)
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: Chernobyl PAZ was 3km initially → too small; contamination hot spots at 60km NW sector; post-Chernobyl international revision: IAEA EPZ now considers site-specific meteorology and reactor type; for RBMK 3000 MWth: EPZ should be 10-20km for planning; ZNPP (Russian occupation): no Ukrainian emergency planning possible; IAEA monitoring team = substitute but not equivalent

details: Urgent Protective Action Zone (UPZ): typically 10-30 km radius; actions: sheltering; KI distribution; evacuation if contamination measured; food/water restrictions; Soviet Chernobyl 30km zone was UPZ equivalent; post-Chernobyl: all reactor sites required to establish and exercise formal EPZ; national Emergency Response Plans required; IAEA assists developing countries with EPZ development
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: 30km zone at Chernobyl: 116,000 persons evacuated; appropriate for preventing major acute doses; did not prevent iodine-131 thyroid doses (contamination extended much farther); reveals limitation: EPZ alone insufficient without: KI pre-positioning; food/water monitoring out to 100km; livestock removal

details: IAEA GSG-2 (2011) Protective Action Levels: sheltering: 10-50 mSv projected dose (effective); KI distribution: 50-500 mGy projected thyroid dose; evacuation: 20-100 mSv projected effective dose; relocation: 20-100 mSv projected effective dose over first month; food restrictions: variable by food type; long-term relocation: >1 Sv total projected; ICRP 103 general recommendations: occupational emergency 20-100 mSv range
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: PAL comparison to 1986 Soviet practice: evacuation threshold 35 rem (350 mSv) = 3.5x IAEA current guidance; explains why Pripyat evacuation delayed 36 hours (dose assessment showed 35 rem not yet exceeded); if current IAEA threshold (20-100 mSv) applied in 1986: Pripyat would have been evacuated IMMEDIATELY on April 26; KI should have been distributed at <10 mGy thyroid

details: Post-Fukushima (2011) EPZ revisions: Japan: expanded monitoring from 20km to 80km in Fukushima; expanded EPZ for future planning; USA: NRC required all sites to re-evaluate EPZ adequacy; most US sites EPZ 10 miles (16km) maintained but back-end planning improved; IAEA: published revised emergency preparedness standards (GSR Part 7 2015); key improvement: mass distribution of KI pre-positioned at schools/homes in EPZ
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: Fukushima showed: 20km EPZ insufficient for BWR at 4000 MWth; contamination extended to 40km (US Embassy recommended 80km); Chernobyl 1986 showed same limitation (30km); recurring pattern: planned EPZ too small for worst-case scenario; nuclear emergency planning inherently challenged because: pre-positioned resources must cover 'design basis' scenario; actual events often exceed design basis

details: Potassium iodide (KI) effectiveness: >90% thyroid dose reduction if taken BEFORE or within 1 hour of exposure; 70% if taken 2-4 hours after; <10% if taken >8 hours after; dose: adult 130 mg (130 mg KI = 100 mg stable I); child: 65 mg; infant: 32 mg; contraindication: thyroid disease; critical: must be PRE-positioned in EPZ; post-accident distribution FAILS because logistics collapse during emergency; Poland 1986 = only success case (pre-positioned; 18M doses distributed Apr 28-29)
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: Chernobyl KI lesson: Soviet failure to pre-position KI in Pripyat = impossible to distribute during 36hr evacuation delay; thyroid doses to children would have been 30-60% lower with KI+earlier evacuation; Poland's success: KI was stocked at pharmacies/schools with emergency authority to distribute; current requirement: IAEA/ICRP recommend KI pre-positioning at all homes within 3-5km EPZ and at emergency centers in 3-30km zone

details: Soviet emergency response 1986: OSNAZ special force for radiological/NBC incidents (military); Go Civil Defense (Grazhdanskaya Oborona); no dedicated civilian NPP emergency response organization; improvised response; comparison: US FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency) established 1979 after TMI; has annual nuclear exercises at every US plant; defined incident command; state/county coordination; Japan: no independent nuclear regulator before Fukushima (same ministry = operator+regulator); post-2012: NRA (Nuclear Regulation Authority) independent
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: Post-Chernobyl: IAEA member states required to establish independent nuclear emergency organizations; Ukraine: SNRIU + Emergency Situations Ministry (2014: State Service of Emergency Situations SESU); integrated into EURDEP for pan-European monitoring; ZNPP emergency response: IAEA monitoring + SNRIU oversight from distance; actual site emergency response = Russian military during occupation

details: INES (International Nuclear and Radiological Event Scale): 0-7 scale; established 1990 (post-Chernobyl); jointly developed IAEA/NEA; Level 7 = major accident: external release large fraction of reactor inventory; Level 6 = serious accident: significant external release; Level 5 = accident with wider consequences; Level 4 = accident with local consequences; Level 3 = serious incident; Level 2 = incident; Level 1 = anomaly; Level 0 = below scale; only two Level 7 events ever: Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011)
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: INES scale designed specifically BECAUSE of Chernobyl: before 1990 no standard way to communicate nuclear event severity; TASS described Chernobyl as 'accident at nuclear station' (equivalent to INES 2-3 language); INES 7 in 1990 terminology: Chernobyl as Level 7 landmark; Fukushima also Level 7 but released ~1/5 of Chernobyl's Cs-137; shows limitation: single number can't capture magnitude difference between two Level 7 events

details: Iodine deficiency interaction with I-131 dose: stable iodine deficiency → thyroid avid for iodide → concentrates radioiodine more effectively → higher thyroid dose per Bq intake; Ukrainian/Belarusian/Russian populations 1986: selenium and iodine deficient due to: Soviet diet (low seafood; low iodized salt); geographic (inland; no seafood access); measured effect: iodine-deficient thyroid concentrates I-131 1.5-3x more than iodine-sufficient; amplification factor for thyroid dose
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: Soviet Union 1986: systematic iodine deficiency in areas of Belarus, Ukraine, Russia receiving most contamination; not a coincidence: same geographic areas (poor soils; inland; low seafood) had highest fallout deposition AND highest iodine deficiency → thyroid doses amplified 1.5-3x; explains higher-than-model-predicted thyroid cancer rates in these populations; see iodine_atmospheric_chemistry_REAL.csv

details: Emergency public communication: modern IAEA standard: notify affected public within 1 hour of emergency declaration; provide protective action recommendations within 2-4 hours; continuous public updates; use multiple communication channels; 1986 Soviet: TASS announcement 66 hours after accident; even then vague; Chernobyl was first post-Chernobyl example of what not to do; Sweden: in 2026 EURDEP monitoring → any similar release detected within minutes → public notification within hours
chernobyl_znpp_relevance: Emergency communication lessons from Chernobyl: (1) delay caused additional exposure (Pripyat May Day parade); (2) public distrust of authorities post-disaster; (3) over-reaction to inadequate information; modern nuclear emergency communication theory: transparent early communication (even incomplete) reduces panic better than delayed complete information; Fukushima Japanese government communication failures (15-year review 2022 showed systematic withholding) = same error repeated
